language_wrapper:
Let f(x), g_k(x), and h(x) be functions on positive integers defined as follows.
- f(x) is the number of integers in the list 1, 2, ..., floor(x/2) that are coprime to x.
- If x = ∏ p_i^{α_i} is the prime factorization of x with the values {p_i^{α_i}} sorted in nonincreasing order p_1^{α_1} ≥ p_2^{α_2} ≥ ..., define g_k(x) to be the k-th largest element of the multiset {p_i^{α_i}}. (If x has fewer than k distinct prime factors, then no b qualifies.)
- h(z) is the least positive integer m such that z divides m!.

Fix integers {e} ≥ 2 and {k} ∈ {1, 2}. Find all integers b > 1 such that

f(b) = h(g_k(b^{ {e} })).

After solving, output the complete set of all such b in the format:
### The final answer is: $\boxed{\{b_1, b_2, \dots\}}$
(list the elements in increasing order, separated by commas).
hardness_rationale: This family generalizes the seed in two orthogonal ways: (i) it raises the exponent inside g from 2 to a tunable e ≥ 2; (ii) it replaces the largest prime power by the k-th largest one (k ∈ {1, 2}), introducing an order constraint among prime-power components. While the seed problem collapses to f(b) = φ(b)/2 equated to h of the largest prime power squared, our variant forces solving φ(b)/2 = h(p_k^{eα_k}) where p_k^{α_k} is the k-th largest prime power in b. This couples the multiplicative structure of φ(b) over all prime-power factors with a single order-selected factor through h; equality translates to a multiplicative Diophantine constraint φ(n) = 2 h(p^{eα}) / φ(p^α) plus rank-order inequalities among prime powers. The solution demands using Legendre’s formula for h, multiplicativity of φ, bounding arguments that for α ≥ 2 the ratio shrinks quickly, and—when k = 2—combinatorial assembly of φ(n) from coprime prime-power totients under strict order constraints. This is appreciably more intricate than the seed’s case-by-case handling for the largest prime power, and guessing is infeasible.
notes:
Proof outline for correctness of the solver and the family (k in {1,2}, e ≥ 2):
1) Basic identities. For any b > 1, the set of residues coprime to b modulo b is symmetric in pairs r and b−r, giving f(b) = φ(b)/2. For y = ∏ p_i^{α_i}, g_k(y) is well-defined as the k-th largest p_i^{α_i} (ties essentially do not occur for distinct primes). For h, Legendre’s formula says v_p(m!) = ∑_{j≥1} ⌊m/p^j⌋, and h(p^a) is the least m with v_p(m!) ≥ a.
2) Reduction to a multiplicative equation. Let b = ∏ p_i^{α_i}, and let p^α be the k-th largest prime power dividing b. Then g_k(b^{e}) = p^{eα} and the condition f(b) = h(g_k(b^{e})) becomes φ(b)/2 = h(p^{eα}). Since φ is multiplicative, write b = p^α n with (p, n) = 1 and obtain
   φ(b) = φ(p^α) φ(n). Hence we get
   φ(n) = T(p,α) := 2 h(p^{eα}) / φ(p^α).
   Therefore, solutions correspond bijectively to pairs (p, α) for which T(p,α) is a positive integer and to factorizations of T(p,α) as a product of terms φ(q^β) with primes q ≠ p; this uses multiplicativity of φ and coprimality of prime-power components.
3) Finiteness and bounds. For α ≥ 2, φ(p^α) = p^{α−1}(p−1) grows exponentially in α, while h(p^{eα}) grows at most linearly in α (indeed h(p^{eα}) ≤ p·eα/(p−1) + O(p)). Consequently T(p,α) decreases rapidly with α, and for each fixed p there is a largest α with T(p,α) ≥ 1; beyond that, 2 h(p^{eα}) < φ(p^α), so no solutions occur. For α = 1 and p > e, one has h(p^e) = e p (only multiples of p contribute), so T(p,1) = 2 e p/(p−1). Integrality forces (p−1) | 2e, restricting p to the finite set of primes ≤ 2e + 1; for p ≤ e, only finitely many small primes remain. Thus the candidate (p, α) are finite.
4) Reconstruction of n. Given a candidate (p, α) with T = T(p,α) ∈ Z_{>0}, any solution n must satisfy φ(n) = T and be composed of pairwise coprime prime powers q^β with q ≠ p. Writing T = ∏ φ(q^β) is equivalent to choosing, for each prime q | T with q ≠ p, at most one exponent β ≥ 1 such that φ(q^β) = (q−1) q^{β−1} divides T and the product equals T; if the same q were chosen twice, coprimality would fail and the totient product would not match φ(q^{β_1+β_2}). This yields a complete classification of n.
5) Order constraints for g_k. For k = 1, require p^α exceeds every other q^β used to build n; otherwise the largest prime power of b would not be p^α. For k = 2, require exactly one of the q^β exceeds p^α and that all others are ≤ that largest value, so that p^α is indeed second-largest. Under these constraints, g_k(b^{e}) = p^{eα} holds.
6) Equivalence. The forward direction follows from multiplicativity and the definition of T. The converse uses the constructed n with φ(n) = T and the order constraints to ensure g_k(b^{e}) = p^{eα}, immediately yielding φ(b)/2 = φ(p^α)φ(n)/2 = h(p^{eα}), i.e. f(b) = h(g_k(b^{e})).
Algorithmic verification mirrors this proof: enumerate finite (p,α), build all φ-factorizations of T into coprime prime-power totients with q ≠ p, impose the k-th largest constraint, and finally double-check equality with direct computations of f(b), g_k, and h. The solver also enforces non-triviality (multiple solutions and at least one moderately large value) to ensure difficulty.
source_question:
Let \(f(x),g(x),h(x)\) be functions defined on the set of positive integers. 
Let \(\left\lfloor \tfrac{x}{2}\right\rfloor\) denote the greatest integer less than or equal to \(\tfrac{x}{2}\).
Define \(f(x)\) to be the number of integers in the list \(1,2,3,\dots,\left\lfloor \tfrac{x}{2}\right\rfloor\) that are coprime to \(x\).
If \(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{k}\) are distinct primes and \(y=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}}\cdots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}\), then
\[
g(y)=\max\{\,p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}},\,p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}},\,\dots,\,p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}\,\}.
\]
For a positive integer \(z\), let \(h(z)\) be the least positive integer \(m\) such that \(z\mid m!\).
Find all integers \(b>1\) such that
\[
f(b)=h\!\big(g(b^{2})\big).
\]
After solving the above problem, please output a set (completely enumerating all elements) as your final answer in the following format:
### The final answer is: $\boxed{\{<your answer>\}}$
Example:
### The final answer is: $\boxed{\{101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110\}}$
Note: Please use enumeration to give your final answer. Do not use descriptive methods (e.g., $\boxed{\{x | 101 \leq x \leq 110\}}$).
The final answer should be given as precisely as possible (using LaTeX symbols such as \sqrt, \frac, \pi, etc.). If the final answer involves a decimal approximation, it must be accurate to at least four decimal places.
source_answer:
Solution: 

When \(b=2^{\beta}\) with \(\beta\ge 7\): 
\[
f(b)=2^{\beta-2},\qquad g(b^{2})=2^{2\beta},\qquad h\bigl(g(b^{2})\bigr)\le 2\beta\cdot 2,
\]
hence \(2^{\beta-1}\le 4\beta\), a contradiction.

When \(b=2^{\beta}\) with \(\beta\le 6\): checking case by case shows that only \(\beta=6\) works, i.e. \(b=64\) is a solution.

When \(b=q^{\delta}\) with \(q\) an odd prime:

\(\bullet\) If \(\delta=1\), then 
\[
\frac{q-1}{2}=f(b)=h\bigl(g(b^{2})\bigr)=2q \ \Rightarrow\ 3q=-1,
\]
no odd prime solution.

\(\bullet\) If \(\delta=2\), then 
\[
h\bigl(g(b^{2})\bigr)=h(q^{4})=\frac{q(q-1)}{2}.
\]
If \(q=3\), then \(h(3^{4})=9\neq \frac{3(3-1)}{2}\), contradiction.  
If \(q\ge 5\), then \(h(q^{4})=4q\), so \(4q=\frac{q(q-1)}{2}\), no odd prime solution.

\(\bullet\) If \(\delta\ge 3\):  
If \(2\delta<q\), then \(2\delta q=\tfrac12 q^{\delta-1}(q-1)\), contradiction.  
If \(2\delta\ge q\), then \(2\delta q\ge \tfrac12 q^{\delta-1}(q-1)\).  
By Bernoulli’s inequality, \(q^{\delta-2}\ge 2+2(\delta-2)(q-1)\), which also yields a contradiction.

Therefore, when \(b\) has only one prime factor, the only solution is \(b=64\).

Now suppose \(b\) has at least two prime factors. Write 
\[
b=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}}\cdots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}},
\]
and let \(\varphi(n)\) denote Euler’s totient function (the number of positive integers less than \(n\) and coprime to \(n\)). Then, for a prime power \(p^{\alpha}\) dividing \(b\),
\[
f(b)=\frac12\,\varphi(p^{\alpha})\,\varphi\!\left(\frac{b}{p^{\alpha}}\right)
=\frac12\,p^{\alpha-1}(p-1)\,\varphi\!\left(\frac{b}{p^{\alpha}}\right)
=\frac12\,p^{\alpha-1}(p-1)\,\varphi(n_{1}),
\]
where \(n_{1}=b/p^{\alpha}\) and \(\gcd(p^{\alpha},n_{1})=1\). Let 
\[
\max\{p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}},p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}},\dots,p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}\}=p^{\alpha}.
\]

\(\bullet\) Case \(\alpha=1\): then
\[
h\bigl(g(b^{2})\bigr)=2p \ \Rightarrow\ 2p=\frac12(p-1)\,\varphi(n_{1}).
\]
But \(p\mid (p-1)\varphi(n_{1})\) is impossible, so no solution.

\(\bullet\) Case \(\alpha=2\): 
\[
f(b)=\tfrac12 p(p-1)\,\varphi(n_{1})=h(p^{4}).
\]
If \(p=2\) or \(3\), no solution.  
If \(p=5\), solving gives \(n_{1}=3\) or \(4\) or \(6\). Since \(\gcd(5^{2},n_{1})=1\), we get \(b=75\) or \(100\) or \(150\).  
If \(p\ge 7\), then \(\tfrac12 p(p-1)\varphi(n_{1})=4p\) forces \((p-1)\mid 8\), which fails; hence no solution.

\(\bullet\) Case \(\alpha=3\): 
\[
f(b)=\tfrac12 p^{2}(p-1)\,\varphi(n_{1})=h(p^{6}).
\]
If \(p=2\), then \(h(2^{6})=8\Rightarrow \varphi(n_{1})=4\). With \(\gcd(2^{3},n_{1})=1\), we get \(n_{1}=5\) and thus \(b=40\).  
If \(p=3,5,7\), we obtain respectively \(9\varphi(n_{1})=15\), \(50\varphi(n_{1})=25\), \(147\varphi(n_{1})=42\), none giving integer \(\varphi(n_{1})\); contradiction.  
If \(p\ge 11\), then \(\tfrac12 p^{2}(p-1)\varphi(n_{1})=6p\) would imply \((p^{2}-p)\mid 12\), impossible; no solution.

\(\bullet\) Case \(\alpha=4\): 
\[
f(b)=\tfrac12 p^{3}(p-1)\,\varphi(n_{1})=h(p^{8}).
\]
For \(p=2,3,5,7,11\), we get respectively
\[
4\varphi(n_{1})=10,\quad 27\varphi(n_{1})=18,\quad 250\varphi(n_{1})=35,\quad 1029\varphi(n_{1})=49,\quad 6655\varphi(n_{1})=88,
\]
none of which yields an integer \(\varphi(n_{1})\); contradiction.  
If \(p\ge 13\), then \(\tfrac12 p^{3}(p-1)\varphi(n_{1})=8p\) would force \((p^{3}-p^{2})\mid 16\), impossible; no solution.

\(\bullet\) Case \(\alpha\ge 5\): 
\[
f(b)=\tfrac12 p^{\alpha-1}(p-1)\,\varphi(n_{1})=h(p^{2\alpha})\le 2p\alpha.
\]
But \(p^{\alpha-2}(p-1)\,\varphi(n_{1})>p^{\alpha-2}>2^{\alpha-2}>2\alpha\), a contradiction. Hence no solution.

Therefore, the positive integers \(b>1\) satisfying \(f(b)=h\bigl(g(b^{2})\bigr)\) are exactly
\[
\boxed{\,40,\ 64,\ 75,\ 100,\ 150\,}.
\]

Answer: \(40,\ 64,\ 75,\ 100,\ 150\).
